newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's disgraced Lebed still eyes presidency.
newsitem.headline: Russia's disgraced Lebed still eyes presidency.

text.p: Alexander Lebed, dismissed as Russia's security chief on Thursday, made enemies at almost every turn in his four-month tenure in the Kremlin but still has his sights firmly set on becoming president.

His sacking, announced by Russian President Boris Yeltsin on nationwide television, was as dramatic as his sudden rise to power after a more than 20-year military career and his shock third place in last June's presidential election.

Even in office he did not hide his presidential ambitions and could now become a charismatic opposition leader with high hopes of fulfilling his main dream -- especially if Yeltsin's heart problems make him unable to stay the course.

Lebed, 46, a reserve paratroop general with a voice like the rumble of guns, had kept journalists and political rivals on their toes since Yeltsin made him his national security adviser and secretary of his influential Security Council on June 18.

The pugnacious-looking Lebed made enemies abroad with outbursts on religion and military matters and ran into protest at home from rivals who accused him of serving his own political ends by signing a controversial peace deal with separatists in breakaway Chechnya.
"Russia does not have an historical tradition of military coups. Thank God we are not Argentina," he said, in comments which provoked a protest from the Argentinian foreign ministry.
Mormons in the United States were outraged by other comments. "All these Mormons are mould and filth which have come to destroy the state. The state should outlaw them," he said.
But he also negotiated an end to the nearly 21-month Chechen conflict, where most of the guns have remained silent since August 31.
His efforts to tackle crime and corruption produced less obvious signs of success.
The West has also slowly been coming round and Lebed took his first steps onto the world stage when he visited NATO headquarters in Belgium on his first trip to the West.
"He struck us as being very thoughtful," one NATO diplomat said of the chain-smoking military man, who turned up in Brussels wearing a smart business suit rather than fatigues.
"Not at all what we were expecting; certainly not a bluff desk-thumping character, but very mild and soft-spoken."

But his presidential ambitions angered others in the Kremlin and a personal feud with Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov exploded on Wednesday when Kulikov said Lebed was plotting a "creeping coup". Yeltsin decided Lebed had to go.
"We have a situation whereby Lebed is splitting the team apart and is carrying out...moves which he did not agree with the president. This is totally unacceptable," he said.
During this year's election campaign, Lebed had deployed his deep bass growl and ramrod-stiff barrack-room bearing in a crusade against chaos and crime.
Lebed was a career soldier who rose through the ranks of the paratroop forces and fought in Afghanistan.
His political career began just a year ago after he was removed as commander of Russia's 14th Army in Moldova and resigned from active service.
Lebed, who hails from a line of Cossack soldiers, had made his name in Moldova in 1992 by quelling fighting between Moldovan forces and separatists on the Dnestr region.
He had became more and more outspokenly critical, not only of hardline Dnestr leaders, but of his Moscow bosses.
He won a seat in the State Duma lower house of parliament in December 1995, representing the garrison town of Tula.

He then went on to run for president, finishing a strong third with 15 percent of the votes. That was enough for Yeltsin to bring him into his team in what he saw as a vote-winning move before the second round runoff.

In his camapaign, Lebed targeted Defence Minister Pavel Grachev and the war in Chechnya as major problems for the country. But the rest of his campaign was a broader one for law and order and to restore Russia's national prestige.

Communist plans to recreate the Soviet Union were senseless, Lebed said. The bureaucracy of communist economics breeds corruption and has left Russia with an over-developed defence sector and obolete, crumbling plant in more profitable areas.
Lebed is married with two sons and a daughter.
